{
 "id": "Q42",
 "sourceFile": "Scheduling of eccentric lower limb injury prevention exercises during the soccer micro-cycle - Which day of the week.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title and authors printed in the accepted-manuscript text (Lovell, Whalan, Marshall, Sampson, Siegler, Buchheit; 'Scheduling of Eccentric Lower-limb Injury Prevention Exercises during the Soccer micro-cycle: Which day of the week?') match the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized, counterbalanced crossover field study in 18 semi-professional outfield players from three teams (17 completed all three trials) over three in-season 6-day micro-cycles. Each micro-cycle was either a control or an eccentric lower-limb injury prevention program (IPP) given 1 day (MD+1) or 3 days (MD+3) after a match. Creatine kinase (CK) fell more slowly after an MD+1 program, while an MD+3 program left CK and hamstring soreness higher on MD+4 and MD+5 than control or MD+1, and peak force and countermovement jump showed no between-trial differences after adjustment.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The study measured CK, soreness and neuromuscular function in one league's semi-professional players over three micro-cycles, and it did not measure injuries or match performance. The same standardized program was given to all players and match loads were not controlled, so the results may not transfer to professional squads, as the authors caution.",
 "synthesisCaution": "The main over-read is to treat the CK and soreness changes as proof that MD+1 scheduling prevents injury or that MD+3 always harms match readiness, when injury and match outcomes were not measured.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2018,
   "citation": "Lovell R, Whalan M, Marshall PWM, Sampson JA, Siegler JC, Buchheit M. Scheduling of Eccentric Lower-limb Injury Prevention Exercises during the Soccer micro-cycle: Which day of the week? Accepted manuscript; journal and pagination not printed in text. 2018.",
   "doi": "10.1111/sms.13226",
   "abstract": "Eighteen semi-professional players were monitored over three 6-day micro-cycles, with an eccentric lower-limb injury prevention program given 1 or 3 days after a match and compared with a control cycle. Creatine kinase, hamstring and quadriceps soreness, isometric strength and jump performance were tracked for five days after each match.",
   "tldr": "Doing the eccentric injury prevention program one day after a match slowed the drop in creatine kinase without raising soreness beyond normal recovery. Doing it three days after a match raised creatine kinase and hamstring soreness on the days before the next match.",
   "methods": "Randomized, counterbalanced crossover study: each player completed a control micro-cycle and two micro-cycles with the program at MD+1 or MD+3 across three in-season weeks. Daily measures were capillary creatine kinase, visual-analogue hamstring and quadriceps soreness, isometric posterior-chain peak force and counter-movement jump, plus GPS external load and session-RPE. Outcomes were analysed with linear mixed models adjusted for baseline and sRPE, and reported as magnitude-based inferences.",

{
 "id": "Q43",
 "sourceFile": "Selecting Metrics That Matter - Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title and authors printed in the text (Bishop, Jordan, Torres-Ronda, Loturco, Harry, Virgile, Mundy, Turner, Comfort; 'Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing') match the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified", "Healthy Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review, with no search method described, of how countermovement jump (CMJ) metrics should be chosen for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and injury rehabilitation testing. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed, but a meta-analysis cited by the authors found maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each), whereas time-based metrics such as flight time and time to peak power changed more after intense exercise and over 24-72 h. Tables 2 and 3 use hypothetical data (20 athletes; 3 athletes) to show how a change is judged against the test's coefficient of variation.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The paper gives no search strategy, so the selection of evidence cannot be reproduced and its completeness cannot be judged. Several recommendations rest on the authors' own experience and on correlations, and the worked examples are hypothetical.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the metric choices as validated for their own squads, or read the hypothetical examples as real athlete results.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Bishop C, Jordan M, Torres-Ronda L, Loturco I, Harry J, Virgile A, et al. Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023.",
   "doi": "10.1519/ssc.0000000000000772",
   "abstract": "The countermovement jump is widely used in strength and conditioning, but no overarching guidance exists on which metrics to choose for each purpose. This article discusses how the metrics chosen differ for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and testing of injured athletes.",
   "tldr": "Choose countermovement jump metrics by purpose: jump height, peak force and peak power for profiling, time-based metrics for fatigue monitoring, and asymmetry and landing force for rehabilitation. Before calling any change real, compare it with the test's coefficient of variation.",
   "methods": "Narrative review, with no search method described. Sections cover the associations of CMJ metrics with strength, linear speed and change-of-direction ability, their sensitivity to neuromuscular fatigue, and their use with injured athletes. Table 1 summarizes acute and 19-week training effect sizes from one study of elite snowboard cross athletes, and Tables 2 and 3 apply the change-versus-CV method to hypothetical group and individual data.",
   "findings": "Jump height, peak force and peak power correlate with strength, linear speed and change-of-direction measures, with correlations varying with whether absolute or relative values are used. A meta-analysis cited by the authors found maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each), while flight time (ES -1.4) and relative net impulse (ES -0.69) changed most immediately after intense exercise, and time to peak power and flight time:contraction time ratio changed most over 24-72 h. In injured athletes the authors suggest landing force and asymmetry measures may be more useful than jump height or peak power.",
   "limitations": "No search strategy is described, so the review cannot be checked for completeness. Several recommendations rest on the authors' anecdotal experience, and Tables 2 and 3 are hypothetical examples of calculation rather than observed data. The running header prints Volume 00 and Number 00, and the PDF gives no DOI or page numbers, so the citation omits them.",
   "practicalImplications": "Select CMJ metrics by purpose: jump height, peak force and peak power for profiling, time-based metrics such as time to take-off, RSI-modified or flight time:contraction time for fatigue monitoring, and asymmetry and landing force for rehabilitation. Before calling a change real, compare it with the test's coefficient of variation: in the worked example a 2.9% jump height change was below a 3.8% CV and so was not counted as real.",
   "athleteDev": "For profiling, jump height, peak force and peak power are reasonable choices because they relate to strength and speed. For fatigue monitoring, add time-based metrics, and check each athlete's own variability before reacting to a change.",
   "rtp": "The review does not set return-to-sport criteria. It notes that asymmetries above 10% have been associated with injury risk in prior work and that peak power did not predict future injury in two cited studies, so a jump test alone should not decide return to sport."
 }
}

 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Athlete Wellbeing", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "American Football", "Basketball"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of recent literature on sleep in athletes, covering barriers to sleep, effects on endurance, anaerobic, sprint, accuracy, reaction time and learning, links to injury and illness, and sleep interventions. The review reports that sleep loss impairs endurance performance, reaction time and accuracy, that sleep extension improves accuracy and some sprint times, and that effects on strength, sprint and anaerobic power are inconsistent. It also cites studies in which short sleep was linked to higher reported injury (70% more in middle and high school athletes sleeping under 8 h) and to infection after rhinovirus exposure in adults.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search strategy is described, so the sources cannot be checked for completeness. Many cited performance studies are small (for example, eight or eleven participants), and most injury data come from retrospective youth studies.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the 8 h sleep benchmark and the nap advice as settled athlete guidelines, but the review says there are currently no athlete-specific sleep duration or quality guidelines.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2017,
   "citation": "Watson AM. Sleep and Athletic Performance. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2017;16(6):413-418.",
   "doi": "10.1016/b978-0-323-65403-6.00024-x",
   "abstract": "Athletes often get less sleep than recommended and may have poor self-assessment of their sleep. This review summarizes recent evidence on barriers to sleep, the effects of sleep on athletic performance, and interventions to improve sleep in athletes.",
   "tldr": "Sleep loss clearly impairs endurance performance, reaction time and accuracy, and many athletes sleep less than recommended. Effects on strength, sprint and anaerobic power are less consistent, and there are no athlete-specific sleep guidelines.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of recent literature on sleep in athletes. Topics include barriers to sleep (training, competition, travel, stress, academic load), performance (endurance, anaerobic and sprint power, accuracy, reaction time, learning and executive function), injury and illness, and interventions such as sleep hygiene, travel scheduling and napping. No search method is described.",
   "findings": "Athletes often sleep under 8 h and may misjudge their sleep; in one study of 103 athletes, most slept under 8 h before competition. Sleep loss impaired endurance performance, reaction time and accuracy in the cited studies, and sleep extension improved accuracy and some sprint times, for example a 9% gain in free-throw accuracy in collegiate basketball players. In middle and high school athletes, those sleeping under 8 h were reported as 70% more likely to be injured, and in adults under 7 h of sleep was linked to nearly three times the rate of infection after rhinovirus exposure.",
   "limitations": "The review gives no search strategy and does not state how studies were selected, so completeness cannot be judged. The authors note the mechanisms linking sleep to performance and injury are poorly defined. The PDF prints a 2017 year, while the Crossref record gives 2024; the printed 2017 journal year is used here, and the DOI should be checked against that record.",
   "practicalImplications": "Athletes who sleep poorly or feel excessively fatigued should be screened for conditions such as insomnia and sleep-disordered breathing, and average sleep should be tracked with a monitor or journal for at least two weeks. Keep training and competition times consistent, limit transmeridian travel to two or three time zones, and use naps of about 30 min early in the day when sleep restriction cannot be avoided.",
   "athleteDev": "For performance, the review supports consistent training and competition times and protected sleep, because sleep loss impairs endurance, reaction time and accuracy. Strength, sprint and anaerobic power results are inconsistent, so sleep should not be expected to produce a fixed change in those measures.",
   "rtp": "The review does not address return to sport. It covers sleep and injury risk in athletes generally, mostly from retrospective youth studies, and gives no guidance on sleep during rehabilitation or after injury."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q46",
 "sourceFile": "Slow wave sleep - a recovery period after exercise.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title and authors printed in the text (Shapiro, Bortz, Mitchell, Bartel, Jooste; 'Slow-Wave Sleep: A Recovery Period After Exercise', Science 1981) match the filename and crossrefTitle.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Sleep laboratory recordings in six young athletes (aged 18 to 26) on four successive nights after a 92 km road marathon, compared with the mean of pre-race and post-race control nights. Total sleep time was longer than control on all four nights, and slow-wave sleep rose as a percentage of sleep on nights 1 and 2 (mainly stage 4 on night 1), while REM sleep fell. The authors conclude that slow-wave sleep increases after a large metabolic stress and support the view that it is a recovery period after exercise.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Six participants, one extreme event and control nights two weeks apart with changing training status leave the effect open to day-to-day variation and a first-night effect. The study measured no muscle function, performance or injury outcomes, so it cannot show that the sleep change speeds recovery.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the rise in deep sleep after a 92 km race as proof that sleep drives recovery or that every hard session needs extra sleep, but the study tested one extreme event in six athletes.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 1981,
   "citation": "Shapiro CM, Bortz R, Mitchell D, Bartel P, Jooste P. Slow-Wave Sleep: A Recovery Period After Exercise. Science. 1981;214:1253-1254.",
   "doi": "10.1126/science.7302594",
   "abstract": "Sleep was recorded in athletes on four successive nights after a 92 km road race and compared with control nights. Total sleep time and slow-wave sleep both increased after this metabolic stress.",
   "tldr": "After a 92 km marathon, six young runners slept longer and had more slow-wave sleep on the next two nights than on control nights. Because it is one extreme event in six athletes, the result shows a sleep response to a very large load, not that sleep speeds recovery.",
   "methods": "Six athletes aged 18 to 26 completed a 92 km road marathon. Their sleep was recorded in a sleep laboratory on the night of the race and on three following nights, and compared with the mean of two pre-race control nights two weeks apart and one post-race control night two weeks later. Records were scored blind by two trained scorers, and repeated-measures analyses compared the post-race nights with control.",
   "findings": "Total sleep time was longer than control on each of the four nights after the marathon (F(4,20) = 21.3, P < .05). Slow-wave sleep as a percentage of sleep increased on nights 1 and 2 (F(4,20) = 44.0, P < .001), mainly from stage 4 on night 1, while REM sleep decreased and sleep onset to stage 2 was shorter on night 1. The authors report no significant change in slow-wave sleep percentage on nights 3 and 4.",
   "limitations": "Only six athletes were studied, and no readaptation night was run before the pre-race control, so a first-night effect cannot be fully excluded; the authors acknowledge this. The subjects were training regularly before the race and had restarted exercising by the post-race control, so training status changed between control and test nights.    "abstract": "This perspective summarizes milestones in the science behind current fluid and carbohydrate recommendations for exercise. It also encourages new research into delivery systems and technology-based personal hydration.",
   "tldr": "Fluid and carbohydrate advice for endurance exercise has changed over a century, and the 2% dehydration threshold is contested in elite runners. The authors propose alginate-encapsulated carbohydrate drinks, but their pilot data are too limited to confirm benefit.",
   "methods": "Perspective piece summarizing historical and recent research on fluid replacement, dehydration and performance, carbohydrate formulation and delivery, dental health, and hydration monitoring technology. It also describes a brief pilot in 16 well-trained Kenyan runners on a 25.1 km run, in which four used alginate hydrogel carbohydrate drinks and data from three were analysed. The authors note that the 2% dehydration threshold lacks ecological validity in elite distance running, and that efficacy of the hydrogel system awaits quantification of its effects on carbohydrate oxidation and gastric emptying.",
   "limitations": "This is an opinion-led perspective, and the journal labels it an International Perspective rather than a systematic review; the choice of cited evidence is not explained. The pilot is small, involves a single run, and is described as ongoing, and the authors cite only indirect evidence for ergogenic effect, such as the drink's use by recent marathon winners.",
   "practicalImplications": "The piece does not show that alginate-encapsulated carbohydrate drinks should replace established drinks.    "athleteDev": "For endurance performance, the literature the authors cite favours maltodextrin and fructose blends approaching a 1:1 ratio, and the piece argues that a fixed 2% body-mass loss is not a reliable performance limit in elite runners. It also reports an ongoing pilot in well-trained Kenyan runners on a 25.1 km run at about 2,000 m altitude, in which runners lost 4.2 +/- 1.0% of body mass (range 2.2-5.9%) and three runners using an alginate hydrogel carbohydrate drink consumed about 291 mL over 95 min with no reported gastrointestinal distress. The authors present the hydrogel delivery system as promising but not yet shown to improve carbohydrate oxidation or gastric emptying.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is an opinion-led perspective with no described search, so the selection of cited evidence cannot be checked. The only original data are a brief pilot with three analysed runners and no performance, oxidation or gastric emptying measures.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the hydrogel pilot and the use of the drink by recent marathon winners as evidence that it improves performance, when the authors say efficacy is unconfirmed and the cited support is indirect.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2018,
   "citation": "Sutehall S, Muniz-Pardos B, Bosch AN, Di Gianfrancesco A, Pitsiladis YP. Sports Drinks on the Edge of a New Era. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2018;17(4):112-116.",
   "doi": "10.1249/jsr.0000000000000475",
   "abstract": "This perspective summarizes milestones in the science behind current fluid and carbohydrate recommendations for exercise. It also encourages new research into delivery systems and technology-based personal hydration.",
   "tldr": "Fluid and carbohydrate advice for endurance exercise has changed over a century, and the 2% dehydration threshold is contested in elite runners. The authors propose alginate-encapsulated carbohydrate drinks, but their pilot data are too limited to confirm benefit.",
   "methods": "Perspective piece summarizing historical and recent research on fluid replacement, dehydration and performance, carbohydrate formulation and delivery, dental health, and hydration monitoring technology. It also describes a brief pilot in 16 well-trained Kenyan runners on a 25.1 km run, in which four used alginate hydrogel carbohydrate drinks and data from three were analysed. No structured search is described.",
   "findings": "Runners lost on average 4.2 +/- 1.0% of body mass (range 2.2-5.9%), and all of them exceeded 2% loss despite access to drinks. The three analysed alginate hydrogel users consumed about 291 mL over 95 min, and no gastrointestinal distress was reported with any drink, including the hydrogel at up to 300 g/L carbohydrate. The authors note that the 2% dehydration threshold lacks ecological validity in elite distance running, and that efficacy of the hydrogel system awaits quantification of its effects on carbohydrate oxidation and gastric emptying.",
   "limitations": "This is an opinion-led perspective, and the journal labels it an International Perspective rather than a systematic review; the choice of cited evidence is not explained. The pilot is small, involves a single run, and is described as ongoing, and the authors cite only indirect evidence for ergogenic effect, such as the drink's use by recent marathon winners.",
   "practicalImplications": "The piece does not show that alginate-encapsulated carbohydrate drinks should replace established drinks. The cited guideline of 30-60 g/h for 1-2.5 h events and up to 90 g/h beyond 2 h still applies, and the 2% dehydration rule should be applied with caution in elite runners who lost 4-6% without symptoms. Because low-pH sports drinks may contribute to dental erosion, the authors suggest considering dental health when choosing a drink.",
   "athleteDev": "For endurance performance, the literature the authors cite favours maltodextrin and fructose blends approaching a 1:1 ratio, and the piece argues that a fixed 2% body-mass loss is not a reliable performance limit in elite runners.
